docs.title: Welcome to GLADOS
docs.text:
GLADOS is an Automated Science Pipeline, allowing for computational research experiments to get aggregated results from multiple experiment runs easily. Currently developed by seniors at Rose-Hulman Institute of Technology, the goal is to develop a system that makes it simple to run experiments and gather relevant data, through a low cost, open-source, community-built project.

When you're on the Rose-Hulman internal network, you can access the deployed project at https://glados.csse.rose-hulman.edu.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: To run an experiment on a running copy of the system, get started here.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
To set up a new machine for development, follow the developer installation guide.

To get familiar with the components of the system, check out the Best Practices guide.

docs.title: About
docs.text:
GLADOS, the Automated Science Pipeline, started when Dr. Jason Yoder, a CSSE Professor at Rose-Hulman Institute of Technology, found himself building the same interface for many different computational research projects over his years of research. Finding a natural need to make this repeated process easier to set up, the project began in 2021 as a senior capstone project, with continuous iterations done by different senior capstone project teams each academic year. The goal is to provide a useful website for people with hard to run experiments that they need to iterate on, as GLADOS will speed up the time running those experiments take while also providing a nice interface to view the experiment results on.

The 2024-25 team completed the Kubernetes system migration and created the scalable VMs server infrastructure. They migrated the database from Firebase to MongoDB and authentication from Firebase authentication to Auth.js. They also improved the system's usability by adding features like default experiments, charting, cancellation, archiving, deletion, collapsing, and expanding experiments.

Below is the most recent poster shown at the Rose Show for the 24-25 year.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
• Why 'GLADOS'?

GLADOS stands for 'General Learning and Automatic Discovery for Operationalizing Science', which is a mouthful, but has a memorable acronym, taking inspiration from the Portal series.

  • What technology does this project run on?

GLADOS uses React and Next.js on the frontend, Python on the backend, and MongoDB for data storage, with Auth.js for account management. The production server currently runs on a Kubernetes cluster within the Rose-Hulman firewall, utilizing multiple machines and VMS also provided by Rose-Hulman, giving Kubernetes enough processing power to properly allocate multiple experiments being run at once.

  • Future goals?

GLADOS aims to become more secure in order to eventually broader its scope to be more open source. In addition, getting GLADOS to be at least semi-functional from a mobile device would allow for more flexibility in its usage. These goals are being handed off to next year's senior capstone project team.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The AddNums experiment is a simple Python script that demonstrates how to set up GLADOS with basic parameters. The script performs basic arithmetic operations (addition and subtraction) on two input parameters (x and y) and writes the results to a CSV file. This experiment showcases two ways to gather additional information: 1. Trial's Extra File: Gathers the designated file that a run of the file generates and places in a zip to be uploaded when the experiment completes 2. Trial Result: Integrates the information from a 2 line csv of headers and values that the file run generates and adds them to the result csv that is being uploaded

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: The script accepts the following parameters via a configuration file: - x: The first integer input for the arithmetic operations. - y: The second integer input for the arithmetic operations.

docs.title: Example Configuration File
docs.text:
[DEFAULT]
x = 5
y = 3

docs.title: Output
docs.text: The script generates a CSV file named AddNumResult.csv in the current working directory. The file contains two rows: 1. Headers: Describes the columns in the CSV file. 2. Values: Contains the results of the arithmetic operations.

docs.title: Example Output
docs.text:
If x = 5 and y = 3, the contents of AddNumResult.csv will be: 

Addition,Subtraction
8,2

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The AddNums script is designed to demonstrate config files and show an output for GLADOS.
  • Both Trial's Extra File and Trial Result functionalities can be used simultaneously to gather and analyze the output data.
  • Ensure that the configuration file (config.ini) is correctly formatted and contains valid integer values for x and y.
  • The generated AddNumResult.csv file will be overwritten each time the script is executed, so make sure to save or rename the file if needed.
  • The script requires Python 3.x and the configparser module to run successfully.

docs.title: Full Python File
docs.text:
import csv
import sys
import configparser

# pylint: disable-next=pointless-string-statement
"""
This experiment demonstrates outputting additional information to a file
and telling the system to gather the data from that file.

There are two different ways to gather additional information from an experiment
    - Trial's Extra File: Gathers the designated file that a run of the file generates and places in a zip to be uploaded when
        the experiment completes
    - Trial Result: Integrates the information from a 2 line csv of headers and values that the file run generates
        and adds them to the result csv that is being uploaded

How to tell if they worked
    - Trial's Extra File: You can download a zip file that contains the different output files specified
    - Trial Result: The result csv downloaded has been expanded with information from the specified file


Example settings for a run that demonstrates this: (Any Fields not specified can be left blank or to whatever their default is)

Info:
Trial Result: AddNumResult.csv
If you want a collection of each CSV this experiment runs:
    Trial's Extra File: AddNumResult.csv
Both can be used at the same time

Parameters:
x, 1, 1, 10, 1
y, 1, 1, 10, 1
"""

# pylint: disable=glados-print-used

def main():
    config = configparser.ConfigParser()
    args = sys.argv[1:]
    configFile = args[0]
    config.read(configFile)
    x = int(config["DEFAULT"]["x"])
    y = int(config["DEFAULT"]["y"])
    with open('AddNumResult.csv', 'w', encoding="utf8") as result:
        writer = csv.writer(result)
        writer.writerow(['Addition', 'Subtraction'])
        writer.writerow([x + y, x - y])

    print("done")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Getting Started From Zero
docs.text:
This page is for a brand-new team member who has nothing set up yet: no accounts, no tools, no repo. It walks from a blank laptop to a running local copy of GLADOS that you can sign in to and run an experiment on. The other developer pages assume most of this is already done.

Read it top to bottom the first time. Afterwards, the Daily workflow section is the only part you will need.

How long this takes

Plan for one afternoon. Most of the time is spent downloading Docker images and waiting for the Kubernetes cluster to come up. Nothing here needs to be done twice.

docs.title: 0. Vocabulary
docs.text:
You will see these words everywhere in the code and docs.

Term Meaning Experiment One submission from the web UI or CLI: a program plus a set of parameters to sweep over. Trial (also "run") One execution of that program with one generated config file. Permutation One combination of parameter values. Each permutation becomes one trial. Runner A short-lived Kubernetes Job that executes all trials of one experiment and writes results back to the database. Frontend The Next.js web app in apps/frontend. Talks to MongoDB directly and calls the backend to start experiments. Backend The Flask app in apps/backend. Its main job is creating runner Jobs. Tilt The tool that builds the three images, deploys them into your local cluster, and hot-reloads on code changes. minikube A single-node Kubernetes cluster that runs inside Docker on your laptop. Dev container A Docker image with every tool preinstalled. VS Code runs your terminal and editor inside it. GridFS The MongoDB feature used to store uploaded experiment files and result zips.

docs.title: 1. Accounts and access to ask for in week one
docs.text:
Ask the previous team or the faculty advisor for these on day one. Some take days to get.

  1. GitHub organization membership for AutomatingSciencePipeline. You need write access to push branches and open pull requests. The task board is the GitHub Project.
  2. The team Discord. The Kubernetes secrets file (secret.yaml) is not in git. The previous team stored it in the private Discord. You cannot run the system locally without it. See step 5.
  3. Rose-Hulman network or VPN access. The production site https://glados.csse.rose-hulman.edu/ is only reachable on campus network.
  4. OAuth app ownership. Sign-in uses Google and GitHub OAuth apps. Find out who owns them and get added as an owner. If the local callback URL is not registered on those apps, local sign-in will fail. See Sign in for the first time.
  5. Server access (later, not week one). The production cluster and the glados-forge development VM are documented under VMs and Deployment.

docs.title: 2. Install tools on your laptop
docs.text: These instructions were last verified on Windows 11 with Docker Desktop. Mac and Linux users skip the WSL parts.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
1. WSL2 with Ubuntu. Open PowerShell as administrator and run wsl --install -d Ubuntu. Reboot, then open "Ubuntu" from the Start menu once to create your Linux user. Confirm with wsl -l -v that Ubuntu shows VERSION 2.
  2. Docker Desktop. Install from https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/. In Settings, enable "Use the WSL 2 based engine" and, under Resources, WSL Integration, turn on integration for Ubuntu.
  3. VS Code with these extensions: "Dev Containers" (ms-vscode-remote.remote-containers) and "WSL" (ms-vscode-remote.remote-wsl).
  4. Git on Windows, and git inside Ubuntu (sudo apt install git rsync). The copy script uses rsync.
  5. Python 3 on Windows, only to run the one helper script in the next step.

Why WSL is required on Windows

Tilt's live update watches files with Linux file events. Files on the Windows filesystem mounted into Docker do not send those events, so hot reload does not work. The project therefore copies the repo into the WSL filesystem and runs the dev container from there.

docs.title: Mac and Linux
docs.text:
1. Docker Desktop (Mac) or Docker Engine (Linux). Give Docker at least 4 CPUs and 10 GB of memory in its settings, because minikube will ask for 3 CPUs and about 8 GB.
  2. VS Code with the "Dev Containers" extension.
  3. Git.

docs.title: 3. Clone the repo
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/AutomatingSciencePipeline/Monorepo.git
cd Monorepo

On Windows, clone it anywhere on your Windows drive. The next step copies it into WSL.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
From the repo root in a Windows terminal:

python .devcontainer/start_in_wsl.py

The script copies the repo to ~/Monorepo inside Ubuntu with rsync --delete, then opens VS Code on that copy. It warns you that it is destructive to the WSL copy. Say yes the first time.

You now have two copies of the repo

The Windows folder you cloned and ~/Monorepo inside WSL are separate. The dev container mounts the WSL copy. Edit, commit, and push from inside the container terminal (or from the WSL copy). If you edit the Windows copy, nothing happens in the running app. Rerunning start_in_wsl.py overwrites uncommitted work in the WSL copy.

docs.title: Mac and Linux
docs.text: Open the cloned folder in VS Code.

docs.title: Everyone
docs.text:
VS Code will show a prompt in the bottom right: "Reopen in Container". Click it. If it does not appear, press F1, type "Dev Containers: Rebuild and Reopen in Container", and run that.

The first time this pulls the gladospipeline/glados-dev-container:main image, which is large. Wait until the VS Code terminal opens with a prompt like codespace ➜ /workspaces/Monorepo. That terminal is inside the container. Every command below is run there.

The container already has Python, Node, Docker CLI, kubectl, minikube, ctlptl, helm, and tilt installed. You should not install those on your laptop.

docs.title: 5. Get the secrets file
docs.text:
Ask the team for secret.yaml and place it at:

kubernetes_init/kubernetes_secrets/secret.yaml

It is listed in .gitignore and must never be committed. It is a Kubernetes Secret named secret-env with these keys. The values are base64 encoded.

Key Used by Purpose FRONTEND_WEBSERVER_PORT, BACKEND_PORT, MONGODB_PORT all Ports. Normally 3000, 5050, 27017. MONGODB_USERNAME, MONGODB_PASSWORD frontend, backend, runner Database login. Must match the root user in helm_packages/mongodb-helm/tilt/values.yaml. AUTH_SECRET frontend Auth.js session signing key. AUTH_GITHUB_ID, AUTH_GITHUB_SECRET frontend GitHub OAuth app. AUTH_GOOGLE_ID, AUTH_GOOGLE_SECRET frontend Google OAuth app. AUTH_URL, AUTH_REDIRECT_PROXY_URL, AUTH_TRUST_HOST frontend Where Auth.js thinks the site lives. For local work this must point at http://localhost:3000. GMAIL_CREDS runner Credentials for the "email me when done" feature.

If nobody can find the file, you can build a new one for local use: copy the structure above, generate a random AUTH_SECRET, create your own GitHub OAuth app with callback URL http://localhost:3000/api/auth/callback/github, and reuse the MongoDB values from the helm values file. Everything else can be a placeholder until you need that feature. The frontend deployment that mounts these keys is kubernetes_init/tilt/deployment-frontend.yaml, so that file is the source of truth for which keys must exist.

docs.title: 6. One-time cluster setup
docs.text:
Run this once per dev container, from the repo root inside the container:

./.devcontainer/post-start.sh

It does four things:

  1. npm i in apps/frontend.
  2. Sets minikube to 3 CPUs and 7800 MB of memory, then deletes any existing minikube cluster.
  3. Creates a fresh cluster with ctlptl create cluster minikube --registry=ctlptl-registry. The registry is what lets Tilt push locally built images into the cluster.
  4. pip installs the Python packages the backend and runner need.

It takes several minutes. When it finishes, minikube status should report the host, kubelet, and apiserver as Running.

Not enough memory?

If cluster creation fails with a memory error, lower the number in the minikube config set memory line of post-start.sh to fit your machine, or raise Docker Desktop's memory limit. A recent teammate ran with 7600 MB.

Never rerun this script casually

It runs minikube delete, which wipes the cluster and with it your local database. Only run it again when you have a fresh container (see Rebuilt container below).

docs.title: 7. Start GLADOS
docs.text:
From the repo root inside the container:

tilt up

Press space to open the Tilt web UI, or go to http://localhost:10350. Tilt builds the frontend, backend, and runner images, installs MongoDB with Helm, and deploys everything. The first build is slow. When the header shows all resources green (10/10), open http://localhost:3000.

What Tilt is running:

Resource What it is Reach it at glados-frontend Next.js app http://localhost:3000 glados-backend Flask API http://localhost:5050 glados-mongodb MongoDB replica set via Helm localhost:30000 fix-minikube-folder-perms-* One-shot jobs that create the MongoDB data folders inside minikube n/a runner Image only. A Job is created from it each time an experiment starts see the experiment walkthrough

You can confirm from the terminal:

kubectl get pods

You should see one frontend pod, one backend pod, and three MongoDB pods (glados-mongodb-0, glados-mongodb-1, glados-mongodb-arbiter-0), all Running.

docs.title: Sign in for the first time
docs.text:
The landing page offers "Sign in with Google" and "Sign in with GitHub". There is no username and password login and no mock login for development. Use a real account.

If sign-in bounces back to the landing page or shows an OAuth error, the cause is almost always one of:

  • AUTH_URL in secret.yaml does not say http://localhost:3000.
  • The OAuth app does not have http://localhost:3000/api/auth/callback/github (or /google) registered as a callback URL.

After you change secret.yaml, Tilt reapplies it, but the frontend pod only reads it at start. Click the refresh arrow on glados-frontend in the Tilt UI to restart it.

Your account is created in the gladosdb database with role user. Roles are user, privileged, and admin. Only an admin sees the "Admin" link in the profile menu. To make yourself admin locally, edit your document in the users collection and set role to admin. The experiment walkthrough shows how to connect to the database.

docs.title: 8. Daily workflow
docs.text:
Once the steps above are done, a normal day looks like this.

  1. Open VS Code on the WSL copy (Windows: open a WSL terminal, cd ~/Monorepo, code .) and choose "Reopen in Container".
  2. In the container terminal, check the cluster is up: minikube status. If it is stopped, minikube start.
  3. tilt up, wait for green, open http://localhost:3000.
  4. Edit code. Frontend and backend changes sync into the running pods automatically. Runner changes rebuild the runner image and apply to the next experiment you start.
  5. When you are done, Ctrl+C in the Tilt terminal, then tilt down. This also uninstalls the MongoDB chart and deletes its volume claims. The database files themselves stay inside minikube under /srv/data/mongo-* (hostPath volumes with the Retain policy), so the next tilt up normally picks your experiments back up. To start from an empty database, see the hard reset in Helpful Commands.
  6. Commit from the container terminal. Branch off main (there is currently no dev branch, despite what older pages say) and open a pull request per Best Practices.

docs.title: Rebuilt container: everything is gone
docs.text:
If VS Code rebuilt the dev container (after a devcontainer.json change, a Docker reset, or a long gap), the new container has no cluster and no pip packages, because those live inside the container. Symptoms:

  • minikube status says the "minikube" host does not exist.
  • kubectl get pods says connection to the server localhost:8080 was refused.
  • Every Tilt resource is red immediately after tilt up.

Fix: stop Tilt, run ./.devcontainer/post-start.sh once, then tilt up again. Your node_modules and source are on the mounted volume and survive.

docs.title: "Error - Backend Offline" in the dashboard sidebar
docs.text: The frontend cannot reach glados-backend on port 5050. Check the backend pod in Tilt for a crash, usually an import error or a MongoDB connection failure.

docs.title: Sign-in loops back to the landing page
docs.text: See Sign in for the first time.

docs.title: Ports 3000 or 10350 do not open in the browser
docs.text: Open the "Ports" tab in VS Code (next to Terminal). Make sure 3000, 5050, and 10350 are forwarded. Remove and re-add a port if it is stuck.

docs.title: Docker is not running
docs.text: The container needs the host Docker daemon. Start Docker Desktop, then reopen the container.

docs.title: MongoDB pods restart or stay Pending
docs.text: Usually memory. Lower minikube memory per step 6, or check kubectl describe pod glados-mongodb-0.

docs.title: Helpful Commands
docs.text:
This page will eventually replace the cheatsheet.md page.

This will be a page describing tasks that are simple but may be helpful to developers in the future.

docs.title: Local development (Tilt + minikube)
docs.text: These all run in the dev container terminal. See Your First Experiment for what each layer does.

docs.title: Start, stop, restart
docs.text:
minikube status                 # cluster up? if "host does not exist", run ./.devcontainer/post-start.sh
minikube start                  # start a stopped cluster
tilt up                         # build + deploy everything, UI at http://localhost:10350
tilt trigger glados-backend     # rebuild/restart one resource (also: glados-frontend, glados-mongodb, runner)
tilt down                       # tear down; uninstalls MongoDB and deletes its volume claims (data files stay in minikube)

docs.title: Look at what is running
docs.text:
kubectl get pods                       # frontend, backend, 3 mongo pods, plus runner-<expId> while experiments run
kubectl get jobs                       # one Job per dispatched experiment
kubectl logs -f deploy/glados-backend  # backend logs
kubectl logs -f deploy/glados-frontend # frontend logs
kubectl logs -f job/runner-<expId>     # runner logs (pod is deleted ~60 s after it finishes)
kubectl describe pod <pod-name>        # why a pod is Pending / ImagePullBackOff / OOMKilled
kubectl delete job runner-<expId>      # clear a stuck or duplicate runner job

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Tilt forwards MongoDB to localhost:30000. The root user and password are under auth in helm_packages/mongodb-helm/tilt/values.yaml.

mongosh "mongodb://<user>:<password>@localhost:30000/gladosdb?authSource=admin&directConnection=true"

db.experiments.find({}, {name:1, status:1, passes:1, fails:1, totalExperimentRuns:1})
db.users.updateOne({email: "you@example.com"}, {$set: {role: "admin"}})
db.dropDatabase()   // soft reset of all local data

Hard reset of the local database: tilt down, then minikube ssh -- sudo rm -rf /srv/data/mongo-1 /srv/data/mongo-2, then tilt up.

docs.title: Joining a node to the cluster
docs.text:
Run the following command on the control-plane.

kubeadm token create --print-join-command

This will give you a command printed to the terminal. You run the given command on the worker you are attempting to join to the cluster.

Example:

sudo kubeadm join 123.123.123.123:1234 --token abcde.123465fiasda --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:1234...abcdef

docs.title: Pipenv usage
docs.text:
To activate the backend python environment in the terminal, run source apps/backend/.venv/Scripts/activate

To activate the documentation python environment in the terminal, run source docs/.venv/Scripts/activate

To disable, run deactivate

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text: You can use command aliases to avoid remembering long, but commonly used terminal commands, or even multiple commands. I (Alan) personally found making aliases for git commands to be useful for general development, even outside of this project. There are many guides online showing how to set up aliases on various terminal environments, it may differ depending on what terminal you use.

docs.title: GLADOS Setup for Developers
docs.text:
We use VS Code dev containers for our developer environment because it greatly simplifies dependency setup.

New to the project?

If you have not set up anything yet (accounts, Docker, WSL, secrets), start with Getting Started From Zero. It covers everything this page assumes and links back here.

There are 2 ways to deploy GLADOS that we will cover in this document:

  1. Gitpod developer environment

  2. Local developer environment via Docker

docs.title: Rose-Hulman VM
docs.text: To make development not intensive on an individual's laptop (because we know how a Rose laptop runs after 4 years), we decided to work with the CSSE department to set up another VM dedicated to GLADOS development where all development environments live, called glados-forge. To learn more about this VM, go to the VMs page.

docs.title: Tilt
docs.text: Tilt is the technology that was found to enable live updating for a Kubernetes-based system. With this enabled, whenever a developer makes a change in any of the images (frontend, backend, or runner), it automatically updates the image and hot refreshes the page to show the change without any manual steps. This saves the process of rebuilding images and increases development speed greatly.

docs.title: VS Code + Dev Containers + SSH
docs.text: VS Code has great integrations with Dev Containers and the ability to connect directly to the GLADOS image that has been spun up on the glados-forge server. All dependencies and extensions for development should also be installed.

docs.title: Using Gitpod
docs.text:
Warning

GitPod (now Ona) recently deprecated their Linux runner. This means that, for now, the GitPod environment does not work. In the meantime, refer to "Local Via Docker" for setting up environments.

From Gitpod.io:

Gitpod is a zero-trust platform that provides automated and standardized development environments in your own infrastructure—whether on your local machine, in your cloud account (VPC), or on-prem. It streamlines coding workflows and boosts collaboration by letting teams spin up secure, preconfigured dev environments quickly and consistently.

So, what does that mean?

We install a program on our virtual machine (glados-forge) and that virtual machine can then spin up new virtual machines dispatched through a web GUI for developers to access.

docs.title: How to use Gitpod
docs.text:
• Go to Gitpod (after you have joined the organization)

  • Click into the "Projects" tab

  • You should see a project called GLADOS, hover over that and click "Create Environment"

Note

You only need to do this the first time, as you can reuse the environment after it was created the first time by clicking the "play" button. Creating multiple environments will use up extra space on the glados-forge VM and could cause problems in the future. Try to only maintain one environment unless there is a specific use case.

  • This will open a new environment for you based on the main branch.

docs.title: If you are on Windows, you have to do the following
docs.text:
1. Press Windows key + R

  2. Type .ssh and then click run

  3. If a file named "config" exists open it, if not create one.

  4. Put the following into that file (make sure to update with your Windows username):

Include "C:/Users/{PUT YOUR USER HERE}/.ssh/code_gitpod_flex.d/config"

  • Now you can click the the "Open VS Code" button

  • After it loads you should be in the Monorepo folder on the dev environment

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Install Docker Desktop

  • Setup Ubuntu in WSL2

docs.title: How to setup
docs.text:
On Windows you have to run the dev container from WSL2 due to Windows not supporting the live updating in Tilt.

Skip step 2 if you are not using Windows!

  1. Clone the Monorepo to your machine

  2. Run the start_in_wsl.py script

    python3 .devcontainer/start_in_wsl.py

  3. Now you should have a VS Code window open to the Monorepo that has been copied to your WSL2 instance

  4. In the bottom right of the VS Code window you should be prompted to open as a dev container, if not press F1 and search for "Rebuild", click "Rebuild and Reopen in Container"

  5. Run the "post-start.sh" script from the .devcontainer folder: 

    ./.devcontainer/post-start.sh

  6. You should then have the Monorepo open inside of a dev container.

  7. Start MiniKube by typing the following:

    minikube start

    This is necessary for Tilt to work.

docs.title: Getting Started with the Monorepo
docs.text:
Now that you are inside of a dev container, we will go over how to get a running copy of GLADOS.

  1. Copy the secret.yaml file into kubernetes_init/kubernetes_secrets

  2. From the root of the Monorepo run the following command:

    tilt up

Note

Make sure the secrets file is present and MiniKube is running (see "How to setup").

  1. Now control + click on the URL that is shown: http://localhost:10350

  2. You will see the Tilt interface, wait for the top to say 10/10, and then go to http://localhost:3000

Now you have a running version of GLADOS!

See Best Practices for tips on how to utilize the system in the best way for development.

docs.title: What if the Tasks don’t run?
docs.text: GitPod may have an issue from time to time with successfully running all the tasks after setting up the environment. Stop and rerun the environment to see if the problem resolved. This should work 99% of the time.

docs.title: What is the ports are not working correctly?
docs.text: Go to the Ports tab in VS Code and make sure that the ports are set to the correct ones. you can delete the port and re-add it to the correct port (e.g. 3000) fix the issue. If that does not work, try restarting the dev container.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Documentation is powered by MkDocs with MkDocs Material, hosted on Github Pages. Pipenv is the package manager the documentation uses.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
For developers, an MkDocs setup is included as part of the dev install script.

Note

The dev install script requires a .env file for any environment variables needed. To create a .env file, copy ".example.env" and make any necessary changes.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
Updating documentation is as simple as updating Markdown files, all contained within the docs folder in the Monorepo.

To preview your chages, follow these steps:

Starting in the root directory, navigate to the outermost docs directory.

cd docs

Create and activate a fresh virtual environment.

python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate

Install the required dependencies.

pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -r requirements.txt

Start up the local dev server to preview changes.

mkdocs serve

docs.title: Deploying
docs.text:
With Github Actions, updates to the main branch will automatically build and deploy the static site to the gh-pages branch.

To deploy manually, run 

pipenv run mkdocs gh-deploy --force

Warning

This updates the gh-pages branch with the static site. Keep in mind, if there are unpublished changes, it will display those changes as well, so beware!

To preview what files will be generated and published, this generates the static website files under docs/site/: 

pipenv run mkdocs build

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
There are many MkDocs Plugins that may be useful while updating documentation, so consider them as this documentation evolves! More information about plugins here.

The Github Action for automatic deployment was found here, slightly changed.

If time allows for it, consider looking at Sphinx instead, for documentation. It seems more advanced, with more features and apparently better code integration with documentation, but may be harder to set up and learn.

docs.title: Proposal: Adding an Auto Mode to the Agentic Plan
1. Summary
docs.text:
The current Agentic Implementation Plan was written last year under the assumption that the AI agent should be trusted as little as possible. Every result is kept away from the agent, and the user has to manually release data before the agent can see it. Following client feedback that this is too strict given how far AI agents have come, we propose splitting agent behavior into two modes:

  • Manual mode: the current plan, essentially unchanged.
  • Auto mode: inside a time-limited, budget-limited session the user opens, the agent can run experiments and read their results without asking each time. Only non-sensitive experiments can be used.

This document explains what we keep from the original plan, what we change or remove and why, and how auto mode would work. The longer-term goal the client described, where the agent tries inputs, looks at the results, and tunes the inputs on its own, is covered as a second phase (Section 6), since it builds on auto mode but adds its own problems.

docs.title: 2. Why the Original Plan Is Strict
docs.text:
The original plan treats the agent and its LLM provider as untrusted (the "CHELL"). Two rules follow from that:

  • S-1 / S-2: the agent never sees experiment results or artifacts. Sensitive results are written to a local "handoff region" instead of being returned to the agent.
  • Consent gesture (§4.3, §5.7): the user must take an explicit action (copy/paste, moving a file, etc.) to release each result to the agent. §5.7 says friction here is deliberate and that requests to make consent easier should be treated with skepticism.

Most of the human-in-the-loop cost in the plan comes from these two rules. In contrast, the plan asks for very little approval on actions: submitting an experiment only needs an audit record (S-8).

This matters for the client's goal. An agent that cannot see results cannot tune inputs. As written, the plan makes the "try, observe, adjust" loop impossible without a human copying results back to the agent after every run.

docs.title: 3. What We Keep
docs.text:
Most of the original plan does not create friction for the user and still makes sense. We propose keeping all of the following in both modes.

Item Section Why we keep it Local MCP facade calling the existing REST API §4.1, §4.3, §6.1 The architecture decision is unrelated to strictness. It reuses the CLI's auth and the existing endpoints. GitHub token introspection for auth §4.1, §6.2 Same as above. No reason to revisit. Functional invariants I-1, I-2, I-3 §3.1 These are about correctness (one call per tool call, no altered arguments, no made-up response data), not about restricting the agent. S-3 Credential confinement §3.2 The agent never needs the token. Keeping it hidden costs the user nothing. S-4 Bounded tool surface (static allowlist) §3.2, §5.3 More important in auto mode. With no human approving each call, the fixed set of tools is the main limit on what the agent can do. S-5 Diagnostic discipline, S-6 Egress confinement §3.2 No user friction, and they protect the token and data from leaking through logs or network calls. S-8 Audit integrity, health check, degraded mode §3.2, §4.2 More important in auto mode. When nobody approves actions as they happen, the audit log is how the user finds out afterward what the agent did. Fail closed, CI checks, refusal tests, SDK telemetry caution §5.4, §5.5, §5.6, §5.8, §5.9 Good engineering practices that apply to either mode. Localhost-only binding for the facade §7 Gaps More important in auto mode, since a spoofed caller would also get auto-mode permissions. The HIGH-sensitivity handoff path §4.3 Kept as the behavior for manual mode, which is the only mode sensitive experiments can use.

docs.title: 4. What We Change or Remove
docs.text:
Item Current Proposed Why S-1 Result confidentiality Absolute: the agent never sees results. Applies to every experiment in manual mode. Sensitive experiments can't enter auto mode at all (5.1). Inside an auto session, the agent sees the results of the experiments it creates. The tuning loop requires the agent to read results. Many experiments (addNums, class projects, benchmarks) have no confidentiality requirement. S-2 Artifact confidentiality Absolute. Same condition as S-1, plus a size cap on anything returned to the agent. Same reason. The size cap keeps large artifacts from flooding the agent's context. Per-result consent gesture Required for every HIGH result. Not needed in auto mode, since only non-sensitive experiments enter it. Kept for manual mode. This is the main source of friction the client objected to. §5.7 "The user is a cooperator, not an obstacle" Treat requests to ease consent with skepticism. Rewrite: friction is still the right choice for sensitive data, but the user decides what is sensitive, per experiment. The client has made this decision explicitly, and it should be recorded in the plan rather than left in conflict with it. §5.2 Default new operations to HIGH Per tool. Keep, and add a per-experiment sensitivity classification that also defaults to sensitive (5.1). Keeps the safe default. Marking an experiment non-sensitive is a one-time choice by the user, not a step for every result. Local log user_approval field Yes/no. Replace with mode and approved_by (user or auto). So the log can tell a user-approved action apart from one auto mode did on its own. Scope: agent quality out of scope §2 Still true for the model's choices, but loop limits (budgets, stopping rules) come into scope. Once the agent can act repeatedly without a human, limiting how much it can do becomes an infrastructure concern.

Nothing is deleted outright. The strict path becomes manual mode, which remains the only option for sensitive experiments.

docs.title: 5. Auto Mode Design
docs.text: Auto mode is not a global switch. It exists only inside an auto session: a time-limited, budget-limited window the user opens around one template experiment. Outside a session, the agent is in manual mode and the original plan applies unchanged.

docs.title: 5.1 Sensitive vs. Non-Sensitive Experiments
docs.text:
Definition. An experiment is sensitive if any part of it (code, input data, configuration, or results) must not be shared with a third-party AI provider. It is non-sensitive if its owner is comfortable with all of it being sent to the agent's LLM provider.

An experiment is sensitive if it meets any of these:

  1. Personal data: it uses or produces data about identifiable people (student records under FERPA, health data, human-subjects research under IRB, survey responses).
  2. Restricted data: its data comes with a license, data use agreement, or NDA that limits who may see it.
  3. Confidential work: its code or results are unpublished, or belong to a sponsor or collaborator who has not agreed to sharing.
  4. Secrets: its code or config files contain credentials, API keys, or internal hostnames.

Everything else is non-sensitive: synthetic data, public datasets, public benchmarks, and course or demo experiments.

Example Classification Reason addNums (example_experiments/python/addNums.py) Non-sensitive Synthetic inputs and outputs Genetic algorithm tuned on a standard benchmark function Non-sensitive No real-world data Classifier trained on a public dataset (e.g., UCI Iris) Non-sensitive Data is already public Model trained on student grades or enrollment records Sensitive Personal data (FERPA) Simulation using a sponsor's proprietary model or data Sensitive Restricted data, confidential work Results a research group has not published yet Sensitive Confidential work Any experiment whose script contains an API key Sensitive Secrets

Rules:

  • The experiment owner sets the classification. GLADOS cannot verify it, so it is the owner's statement, and it is recorded in the audit log.
  • Every experiment is sensitive by default (following §5.2 of the original plan). The owner has to mark it non-sensitive.
  • Only non-sensitive experiments can be used in auto mode. Sensitive experiments stay in manual mode, where S-1, S-2 and the consent gesture from the original plan still apply.
  • The agent cannot change any experiment's classification.

This is the main change from the first draft of this proposal. Sensitivity no longer hides some results inside auto mode. Instead it decides which experiments can enter auto mode at all, and inside a session the agent can see every result it produces.

docs.title: 5.2 What the Agent Can and Cannot Do
docs.text: The agent CAN The agent CANNOT Read the configuration of the session's template experiment (parameters, ranges, description) See or act on any experiment outside its current session, including the user's other experiments and other users' Create new experiments from the template, changing only hyperparameter values within the session's bounds Upload, edit, or replace experiment code, or change which files an experiment reads or writes Start the experiments it created, within the session limits Modify the template experiment itself Check the status of its session's experiments Delete experiments or results, including its own Read the results of its session's experiments (result CSV, pass/fail counts, short error summaries) Start, extend, or end a session, or change its limits or parameter bounds Cancel its session's experiments Change any experiment's sensitivity classification See how much of the session's budget is left Use a sensitive experiment as a template Set workers or timeout above the session caps Access the token, read files by path or URL, or reach anything other than the GLADOS REST API (S-3, S-4, S-6) Take any auto-mode action after the session ends (it falls back to manual mode)

docs.title: 5.3 Auto Sessions
docs.text:
Starting a session. The user starts a session outside the agent, for example with a CLI command. There is no MCP tool for it. When starting, the user chooses:

  • Template: one of their own non-sensitive experiments. The agent's experiments are copies of it with different parameter values.
  • Parameter bounds: which hyperparameters the agent may change, and the allowed range for each.
  • Limits: the values in 5.4. If the user doesn't set them, the defaults apply.

Session boundary. The server tags every experiment the agent creates with the session ID and checks that tag on every request. Because the check happens on the server and not only in the local facade, the boundary still holds if the facade restarts. Each experiment belongs to exactly one session, and the agent can only see experiments from its current session.

Ending a session. A session ends at the first of:

  • the user ends it,
  • the time limit runs out,
  • the experiment or trial budget runs out, or
  • the audit log becomes unavailable (degraded mode, original plan S-8).

When a session ends, the agent loses auto-mode access immediately. Queued experiments are cancelled, and running experiments finish normally. If the user ends the session with a "stop all" option, running experiments are cancelled too. Everything created in the session stays in the user's account like any other experiment.

docs.title: 5.4 Session Limits
docs.text:
These are proposed starting values. They need client input (Section 9).

Limit Proposed default Enforced by Reason Session length 4 hours Server No session runs unattended indefinitely Experiments created per session 10 Server Caps the number of rounds Total trials per session (sum over all experiments) 500 Server One experiment can expand into many trials through parameter ranges Experiments running at once 2 Server Leaves cluster capacity for other users workers per experiment No more than the template's value Server The agent can't claim more parallelism than the user chose timeout per trial No more than the template's value Server Same reason Tool calls 30 per minute, 1,000 per session Facade Stops a runaway agent and protects the GitHub 5,000 requests/hour limit Status checks At most once every 30 seconds per experiment Facade Polling is the most likely source of excess calls Result size returned to the agent 64 KB per call Facade Keeps responses predictable. Larger results are cut off, with a note saying so

When a limit is reached, the request is refused with a short reason, such as "trial budget exhausted." Following the fail-closed rule (original plan §5.5), it is never partly carried out.

The agent's own LLM token use happens on the agent's side, where GLADOS can't see or limit it. The tool-call limit is the closest control GLADOS has.

docs.title: 5.5 Security Carried Over from the Original Plan
docs.text: Original rule In auto mode S-1, S-2: the agent never sees results or artifacts Replaced by the admission rule in 5.1: sensitive experiments never enter auto mode. Still applies in full to manual mode. S-3: credential confinement Unchanged S-4: fixed tool list, no free-form paths or URLs Unchanged, and extended: parameter values must fall within the session bounds S-5, S-6: logs and network restrictions Unchanged S-8: audit integrity Unchanged. No session action completes without an audit record. I-3: responses carry nothing the REST API didn't return Unchanged. The size limit only cuts results off, and says so. Fail closed, localhost-only facade Unchanged

docs.title: 5.6 One Auto Mode Iteration
docs.text:
GitHub token checks happen on every REST call, as in the original plan §4.1. They're left out of the diagram for readability.

sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    participant Agent as AI Agent (CHELL)
    participant MCP as MCP Facade
    participant REST as REST API
    participant Audit as Audit Log
    participant Runner as Runner

    User->>MCP: start session (template, bounds, limits)
    Note over User,MCP: Out of band, not an agent tool
    MCP->>REST: create session
    REST->>REST: check template is non-sensitive and owned by user
    REST->>Audit: log session start (bounds, limits)
    Audit-->>REST: written
    REST-->>MCP: session ID

    Agent->>MCP: create_run(new parameter values)
    MCP->>MCP: check call rate and session is active
    MCP->>REST: create experiment from template (session ID)
    REST->>REST: check session, bounds, budget, concurrency
    alt check fails
        REST-->>MCP: refused (reason only)
        MCP-->>Agent: refused (reason only)
    else check passes
        REST->>Audit: append record
        Audit-->>REST: written
        REST->>Runner: start experiment
        REST-->>MCP: experiment ID, budget left
        MCP-->>Agent: experiment ID, budget left
    end

    loop at most once every 30 s
        Agent->>MCP: get_status(experiment ID)
        MCP->>REST: get status
        REST-->>MCP: status
        MCP-->>Agent: status
    end

    Agent->>MCP: get_results(experiment ID)
    MCP->>REST: get results
    REST->>REST: check experiment belongs to this session
    REST-->>MCP: result CSV
    MCP->>MCP: drop unknown fields, apply size limit
    MCP-->>Agent: results
    Agent->>Agent: choose next values (Phase 2) or report to user (Phase 1)

docs.title: 5.7 Audit and Invariant Changes
docs.text:
Audit records gain session_id, mode, approved_by (user or auto), and template_experiment_id. Session start and end are also logged, with the bounds and limits chosen and the reason the session ended.

Invariants:

  • S-1, S-2: apply to all experiments in manual mode. In auto mode they are replaced by S-9.
  • S-9 Admission: only experiments the owner marked non-sensitive can be session templates, and every experiment created in a session inherits that classification.
  • S-10 Session boundary: the agent can only read or act on experiments tagged with its current, active session.
  • S-11 Limits: no action that would exceed a session limit is carried out.
  • S-12 User control: sessions, bounds, limits, and classifications are set only by the user, never through an agent tool.

Each one can be tested in CI the same way as original plan §5.6, by attempting every CANNOT action in 5.2 and checking that it is refused.

docs.title: 6.1 Phase 1: Auto Mode Infrastructure and Permissions
docs.text:
Goal: the agent can run experiments and read results inside a session, one step at a time as the user prompts it (for example, "try x from 1 to 20 and tell me what you see").

In scope:

  • Sensitivity classification on experiments, defaulting to sensitive
  • Starting and ending sessions, with session tagging and server-side checks
  • The session limits in 5.4
  • MCP tools for each action in the CAN column of 5.2
  • The audit and invariant changes in 5.7
  • Tests showing every CANNOT action is refused (original plan §5.9: test refusals, not just success)

Out of scope: the agent deciding on its own what to run next, objectives, and stopping rules.

Done when: with addNums as the template, an agent can create, run, and read results for experiments in a session, and tests show every CANNOT action in 5.2 is refused.

docs.title: 6.2 Phase 2: Automatic Tuning Loop
docs.text:
Goal: the user states a goal once, and the agent runs several rounds on its own without a prompt between rounds.

Adds:

  • Objective: the user names one result column to maximize or minimize when starting the session.
  • Stopping rules: the loop stops when the target is reached, when there has been no improvement for N rounds, or when the budget runs out. The facade enforces these, since it sees every result. Trusting the agent to stop on its own would go against original plan §5.1.
  • Coarse-to-fine rounds: GLADOS already runs every combination of a parameter's min/max/step range (apps/runner/modules/configs.py). So each round is one experiment: a wide grid first, then narrower ranges around the best results.
  • Round history: each round records its parameter values, its best result, and the round it came from, so the user can see how the agent reached its answer.
  • Final report: the best parameter values found and the round history, returned to the user when the loop stops.

Out of scope: multiple objectives, parameters not in the template, and changes to experiment code.

Done when: given a template and an objective, the agent completes at least three rounds, stops on its own by one of the stopping rules, and every round appears in the audit log.

docs.title: 6.3 Why This Split
docs.text: Phase 1 is useful by itself. Even without a loop, a user can ask the agent to run a few variations and compare them. It also builds every permission the loop relies on. Phase 2 adds no new permissions: it only adds the objective, stopping rules, and round history on top of Phase 1.

docs.title: 7. Risks and Tradeoffs
docs.text:
• Results reach the LLM provider. This is accepted by design for non-sensitive experiments. Sensitive experiments can't enter auto mode.
  • Owners may misclassify experiments. The default is sensitive, so a mistake means marking something non-sensitive on purpose. The audit log records who marked it and when.
  • Prompt injection through results. A result file could contain text that tries to steer the agent. The fixed tool list, session boundary, limits, and the no-delete rule limit what a steered agent can do.
  • Less oversight while a session runs. Offset by the session limits and audit records. The tradeoff is reviewing after the fact instead of approving each action.

docs.title: 8. Proposed Milestones
docs.text:
1. Revise the original plan's sections listed in Section 4, after this proposal is approved.
  2. Build the MCP facade with manual mode as specified in the original plan.
  3. Phase 1: sensitivity classification, auto sessions, session limits, and audit changes.
  4. Test end to end with addNums in both modes (original plan §8.1).
  5. Phase 2: the tuning loop.

docs.title: 9. Questions for the Client
docs.text:
1. Is the owner's own classification enough, or should non-sensitive status be confirmed by an admin or tied to something like IRB status?
  2. Are the default limits in 5.4 reasonable for the cluster? Should admins be able to set per-user maximums?
  3. Should the agent be able to read the template's code and trialExtraFile archives, or only the result CSV? Code helps it understand the parameters, but sends more to the provider.
  4. When a session ends, should running experiments finish or be cancelled?
  5. Should auto mode be open to all users, or only privileged/admin users at first?
  6. For non-sensitive experiments, is it acceptable that the LLM provider may retain the data under its own policies?

docs.title: 1. Problem and Context
docs.text:
With the successful launch of the CLI, the next step is to make the GLaDOS platform compatible with Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool calls so that experiments can be carried out be autonomous Artificial General Inteligence (AGI) agents. Specifically, the goal is to give the user the ability to delegate actions they can take on the platform manually to an AI agent that performs them on their behalf.

After some consideration, the team decided that it is recommended to pursue a local MCP facade that calls to existing REST endpoints with authentication done via token introspection. For more details on this decision consult section 5 and 6 of this document.

docs.title: 2. Scope and limitations
docs.text:
The following describes both the scope of the agentic implementation feature as well as possible limitations:

  • The agentic model used by the user is not within scope; the mistakes the model might make in utilizing MCP tool calls or in adjusting the hyperparameters of an experiment for a new run is not within scope. Ergo, the infrastructure for such calls to occur securely and consistently is within scope; the quality of the model is not.
  • The user of this feature is assumed to have a GitHub account for which a GitHub token can be gained through device flow authentication, which allows for authentication to GLADOS; Google OAuth or other provider specific Oauth routes are not within scope.
  • We recommend limiting this feature to user's of priviledged or admin permission levels, however this feature does have the possibility to be open to users at all permission levels.
  • All operations requires a verification step via GitHub api, users who hit their GitHub api limit of 5000 requests per hour will not be able to access MCP features and have to use the browser GUI manually

docs.title: 3. Invariants
docs.text: Let t be an MCP tool call, and ENDPOINT be an authenticated call (using a stored token for the active session) to the existing REST API counterpart for t.

docs.title: 3.1 Functional Invariant
docs.text:
For all tool invocation with arguments t(args), the following premises must hold:

I-1 - Structural. The invocation of t(args) causes exactly one ENDPOINT call to be reported to the caller. The MCP MAY retry on transport failure up to a bounded number of times before surfacing failure; retries are not counted as separate logical calls.

I-2 - Payload. Content of args must not be modified beyond translation to comply with ENDPOINT argument schema. A translation here is defined as a syntactic transformation using a declared schema, no values should be transformed.

I-3 - Response Content. Given that the MCP tool call is going to translate the REST response into an MCP response, the MCP response carries no information not present in the REST response; fields may be dropped, but never fabricated, inferred, or sourced from outside the REST response.

docs.title: 3.2 Security Invariant
docs.text:
The LLM agent and its provider sit outside of GLADOS's trust boundary and are therefore modeled as a Compromisable Host or External LLM Liaison (CHELL). The following invariants must hold against the CHELL:

S-1 - Result Confidentiality. CHELL shall not gain read access to result data returned by any ENDPOINT call. MCP responses, error messages, transport metadata, and diagnostic output shall not carry result content to CHELL.

S-2 - Artifact Confidentiality. CHELL shall not gain read or write access to artifacts that a tool call requires or produces. Artifact content reaches CHELL only through channels the user explicitly drives (e.g., paste, upload).

S-3 - Credential Confinement. The token shall not be observable by CHELL through any MCP tool result, error path, argument echo, or diagnostic output.

S-4 - Bounded Tool Surface. CHELL may only invoke t drawn from a statically declared allowlist. No t shall accept free-form filesystem paths, URLs, shell expressions, or ENDPOINT specifiers as arguments. This prevents CHELL from inducing arbitrary reads, writes, or egress through args.

S-5 - Diagnostic Discipline. MCP facade logs, stderr, crash output, and telemetry shall not contain result data, artifact content, or credential material in any form CHELL or its host can read.

S-6 - Egress Confinement. The MCP facade shall initiate no outbound network connection other than to ENDPOINT over verified TLS. CHELL shall not be able to induce arbitrary egress through args.

S-7 - User Override. Voluntary delivery of data to CHELL by the user (paste, upload, screen sharing, dictation) lies outside the protection of S-1 … S-6. The facade shall neither facilitate, conceal, nor attempt to detect such transfers.

S-8 - Audit Integrity. No state-mutating tool call shall complete without a corresponding append-only audit record being durably written. Records shall be neither modifiable nor deletable through any system interface. The audit log shall contain no silent gaps: any period during which audit writes were unavailable shall itself be reflected in the log as a degraded-mode record.

docs.title: 4.1 Authentication Subsystem
docs.text:
The system establishes caller identity at the REST API via RFC 7662 token introspection. The MCP facade is the sole custodian of the user's token within the local environment; this placement is what realizes S-3 (credential confinement).

No MCP tool surface can expose the token to CHELL, by construction.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
1. AI agent (within CHELL). Issues MCP tool calls. Never observes the token.
  2. MCP facade. Holds the token, attaches it to REST calls, translates responses per I-2 and I-3, returns them to the agent subject to Section 3.2.
  3. REST API. Validates the token via introspection, resolves identity, executes the requested operation under the resolved identity. GitHub. Issues the token and serves the RFC 7662 introspection endpoint. Source of external identity.
  4. MongoDB. Maps external (GitHub) identity to internal system identity U. Source of truth for per-user authorization.

sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    participant Agent as AI Agent (CHELL)
    participant MCP as MCP Facade
    participant REST as REST API
    participant GH as GitHub
    participant DB as MongoDB

    User->>Agent: prompt: task A on data D
    Agent->>MCP: t(ref(D))
    Note over Agent,MCP: S-2: D passed by reference
    MCP->>REST: request task A (Authorization: Bearer <token>)
    Note over MCP,REST: S-3: token held only by MCP
    REST->>GH: POST /introspect (token)
    GH-->>REST: { active, external identity }
    REST->>DB: lookup(external identity)
    DB-->>REST: internal identity U
    REST->>REST: execute task A as U
    REST-->>MCP: result
    MCP-->>Agent: translated result (subject to S-1)
    Agent-->>User: response
1. User prompts the AI agent to perform task A on data D. 2. The agent invokes the corresponding MCP tool with a reference to D, not its contents (S-2). 3. The MCP facade issues a REST call for task A with the token attached (per I-2). 4. The REST API introspects the token at GitHub and receives the external identity. 5. The REST API resolves external identity to internal identity U via MongoDB. 6. The REST API executes task A under U and returns the result. The facade translates the response per I-3 and surfaces it to the agent subject to S-1.

docs.title: 4.2 Audit Logs
docs.text: To appropriately log the actions of the agent, we recommend a two-pronged approach with an audit log both locally available for a user as well as a remote audit log for GLADOS's server. This ensures that the user can reread the local log to be aware of the actions of the agent, and developers can monitor agent activity via the remote log.

docs.title: 1. Remote Audit Log
docs.text:
Creating a new capped collection on GLADOS’s MongoDB with role-based restrictions that prevent editing operations is our recommended implementation of a synchronous append-only sink.

In this collection, record an agent request’s event_id, user_id, timestamp, action_type, action_result, and agent_id. A successful write/insertion to the collection allows the request to go through (the action to occur on the server); otherwise, the request is denied. A health check, implemented by a ping command to the database via a Next.js endpoint on GLADOS’s server, checks if an insertion could happen to the collection; if the check returns unhealthy, allow agentic non-mutating requests (i.e. read operations) but return degraded-mode error on mutating requests.

The following subsections provide more implementation details on the above description.

docs.title: Document Fields:
docs.text:
For this collection, we recommend enforcing that each of the documents have the following fields for ensuring an accurate and thorough log of agentic activities is recorded:

  • event_id — Unique identifier for each audit event
  • user_id — Unique identifier for the user who initiated the action
  • timestamp — UTC timestamp indicating when the action occurred
  • action_type — Type of action performed (e.g., file_read, file_write)
  • action_result — Outcome of the action (e.g., success, failure)
  • agent_id — Identifier of the agent or model that performed the action

docs.title: Synchronous:
docs.text: In this setup, when an agent sends a request via an endpoint to GLADOS, an entry would be made in the MongoDB collection reflecting the event. And once this insertion is successfully made, the requested action can go through. Otherwise, the action would fail as the log insertion was not successful.

docs.title: Append-Only:
docs.text:
Developers should restrict editing or delete permissions for this collection- this log is intended as a non-mutable record of events. Should a correction need to be made, a new entry should be inserted.

To implement this, developers can use a capped MongoDB collection, which is a type of collection ideal for maintaining logs because delete operations are restricted and, when the fixed size of the collection is reached, old entries are overwritten, which is ideal for audit logs as the most recent entries are most valued. Additionally, edit operations from users should be restricted via role-based checks in GLADOS server endpoints.

docs.title: Continuous Health Check:
docs.text:
The MCP endpoint can ping the database to ensure that the audit log is healthy can be inserted into. Should this ping fail, agent action requests should be rejected automatically as the log cannot be inserted into. Otherwise, successful health checks mean that the database is healthy and ready for insertion.

To implement this, developers can create a Next.js health check endpoint that pings the MongoDB pod every certain time increments.

docs.title: 2. Local Audit Log
docs.text:
While the current CLI produces a brief log of results/errors as the user runs commands, given the nature of agents, users likely would expect a more thorough record in order to examine what actions the agents took while utilizing their account. Utilizing the Python logging module may be most effective and allow flexibility. The module allows to write to a user’s local file to implement more extensive logging beyond the CLI’s current printouts to the console. Record agentic actions, including datetime, action_taken, user_approval, result (Success or Failure), error (High Level Description Based Off Stack Trace If it Exists), to ensure that the dynamic information is included efficiently within a file that can then be scanned for certain keywords.

A basic logging example is the following: 

>>> import logging 
>>> logging.basicConfig( 
...    filename='glados_audit.log', 
...    level=logging.INFO, 
... ) 
>>> logging.error("Something went wrong!")

By saving the logs to a file, such as “glados_audit.log” as in the above example, instead of simply printing to a terminal, we can ensure that the dynamic information is included efficiently within a file that can then be scanned for certain keywords.

docs.title: 4.3 MCP Facade
docs.text: The system follows a facade architecture: a local process on the user's machine sits between the agent (running under the Claude Code TUI, or any equivalent host) and the remote REST API. The facade is the only component that holds credentials, makes outbound REST calls, and decides what crosses the trust boundary to the agent. Data classified high-sensitivity does not flow to the agent through facade responses; instead, the facade places it in a handoff region on the local filesystem, and the user performs an explicit gesture to release it. The mechanism for that gesture is intentionally underspecified at this layer; suggested implementations are listed below.

docs.text:
flowchart TB
    User((User))

    subgraph LocalHost["Local host (user's machine)"]
        TUI["Claude Code TUI<br/>(user-facing surface)"]
        MCP["MCP Facade<br/>(token custodian, allowlisted tools)"]
        FS[("Artifact handoff region<br/>(filesystem)")]
    end

    subgraph CHELLBox["CHELL (untrusted)"]
        Agent["AI Agent + LLM provider"]
    end

    subgraph Remote["Remote infrastructure (GLADOS)"]
        REST["REST API"]

    User -->|prompt| TUI
    User -->|reviews| FS
    User -.->|consent gesture| FS
    TUI <-->|input / output stream| Agent
    Agent -->|MCP tool calls| MCP
    MCP -->|LOW data response| Agent
    MCP <-->|TLS, bearer token| REST

- Claude Code TUI. User's terminal interface to the agent. Treated as a trusted surface for input/display; does not enforce policy itself. - AI Agent + LLM provider. The reasoning and tool-invocation loop. Modeled as CHELL — anything the agent observes is assumed to be observable by an adversary. - MCP Facade. Local process. Holds the REST API credentials, exposes a static allowlist of tools, and decides per tool whether the result returns inline (low-sensitivity path) or via the handoff region (high-sensitivity path). - Artifact handoff region. A filesystem location where the facade deposits high-sensitivity results. The release of content from this region to the agent is mediated entirely by the user. REST API. Remote service; authenticates via token introspection, authorizes per-identity.

docs.title: Data paths
docs.text:
• LOW - Low-sensitivity path. Agent → MCP tool call → REST → translated MCP response → agent. Constrained by S-1 (no high-sensitivity content in responses) and §3.1 (response translation).
  • HIGH - High-sensitivity path. Agent → MCP tool call → REST → artifact written to handoff region. The agent receives only an acknowledgement; the result content sits at rest until the user acts.

docs.title: Consent gesture - suggested mechanisms
docs.text:
The architecture does not mandate a specific gesture; future contributors should pick what fits their platform. Non-exhaustive options:

  • Copy / paste. User pastes artifact content into the TUI. Unforgeable; manual.
  • Permission flip (chmod). User grants the agent's runtime UID read access; an allowlisted tool then fetches. Requires UID separation between facade and agent.
  • Move into a watched inbox. User drops the artifact into a designated directory the agent reads on demand. Same UID consideration as above. Confirmation token. User reviews the artifact, types a short token displayed alongside it into the TUI; facade releases on next reference. Adds binding/expiry complexity.
  • Out-of-band CLI helper. User runs a small command that pushes content into the agent's input stream. Useful where clipboard integration is poor.

These are not mutually exclusive, a system may offer several.

docs.title: 5. Implementation notes
docs.text: Some useful implementation notes

docs.title: 5.1 Strive for enforcement through architecture and design rather than prompt engineering
docs.text: An LLM at the end of the day is a probabilistic model. Because of that, banking on the fact that it output will be governable and deterministic is a naive assumption. If you wish for the agent to not attempt an action, then the architecture should never allow for such cases.

docs.title: 5.2 Default new operations to HIGH sensitivity
docs.text: Sensitivity classification is the most consequential decision per tool: LOW means the result flows directly to CHELL. Defaulting to HIGH forces contributors to argue explicitly that a given response field is safe to expose, and creates an auditable trail of those arguments. LOW-by-default silently leaks whatever a less careful contributor didn't think to question.

docs.title: 5.3 Allowlist, never blocklist
docs.text: The set of tools, response fields, and outbound destinations the facade may emit must be statically enumerated. Resist any pattern that lets configuration, runtime conditions, or model output expand these sets. Every such pattern is a path by which CHELL or a misconfigured deployment widens the attack surface.

docs.title: 5.4 Treat error paths like response paths
docs.text: The agent reads errors as eagerly as it reads successful responses. A stack trace, an exception message, or a "field X was missing" complaint is a data channel. The invariants on response content (S-1, S-3, S-5) apply equally to every place the facade can emit text (exceptions, transport errors, debug output, etc...).

docs.title: 5.5 Fail closed
docs.text: When in doubt (introspection times out, schema validation fails, the audit sink is unavailable, an argument is unrecognized) reject the call. A broken feature is recoverable; a silent leak is not. This is the default that makes S-1 (unknown fields dropped) and S-8 (no mutation without audit) cheap to implement: when behavior is ambiguous, the safe answer is to do nothing.

docs.title: 5.6 Encode invariants as CI checks
docs.text: Formal invariants are written to be mechanically translatable. Every invariants that admits a test should have one wired into the CI pipeline: shape assertions for S-1, emit-path scanning for S-3, static analysis of the tool registry for S-4, failure-injection on the audit sink for S-8, and so on. This moves security from contributor discipline (which decays under deadline pressure) to executable proof (which is regenerated on every commit), and makes audits cheap by giving reviewers running tests rather than arguments. The residual judgment (recognizing when a new tool introduces a surface no existing test covers) cannot be mechanized, but it becomes narrower and more honest once routine checks are automatic.

docs.title: 5.7 The user is a cooperator, not an obstacle
docs.text: The high-sensitivity consent gesture exists because the user is a participant in the security model, not friction to be optimized away. Future requests to "make consent easier" by weakening the gesture should be treated with skepticism. UX friction in the consent mechanism is a deliberate choice.

docs.title: 5.8 Beware third-party SDK telemetry
docs.text: Logging libraries, error trackers, and observability SDKs frequently capture function arguments, request bodies, and stack-local variables. Any such SDK installed in the facade process becomes part of S-5's threat surface. Audit every dependency for outbound behavior; prefer libraries with explicit, controllable telemetry.

docs.title: 5.9 Test refusal, not just success
docs.text: The interesting tests in this system are the ones that confirm the facade won't do something: malformed args are rejected, unknown response fields are dropped, audit failure blocks the mutation. Tests that only exercise the happy path leave the actual security properties unverified.

docs.title: 6. Alternatives Considered
docs.text: This section details alternative implementations that were considered during initial architecting and design of the agentic workflow integration.

docs.title: 6.1 MCP as an extention of the current Next.js REST API
docs.text: Rather than running the MCP facade locally on the user's machine, MCP tool calls could be served directly from the existing Next.js REST API, with clients connecting over the network.

docs.title: Why not adopted
docs.text: The REST API authenticates callers by introspecting GitHub-issued tokens (Secion 6.2). In a co-hosted model, the MCP transport would need to deliver those tokens from client to backend. However, MCP's transport-level authorization, defined in the MCP authorization specification, is OAuth-based and does not accommodate passing arbitrary upstream credentials. Adopting this alternative would require either re-implementing the backend's authentication layer to comply with the MCP authorization spec, or inventing a non-standard credential-passing mechanism that would break compatibility with conforming MCP clients. The current team judged the local-facade approach preferable, as it preserves the introspection-based auth model unchanged and reuses REST endpoints without modification.

docs.title: Conditions to reconsider
docs.text: This decision should be revisited if the system migrates authentication to a flow compatible with the MCP authorization spec, or if operating a per-user local facade becomes a deployment burden disproportionate to the cost of MCP-spec auth compliance.

docs.title: 6.2 Self-issued JWTs in place of GitHub token introspection
docs.text: Rather than delegating authentication to GitHub and introspecting GitHub-issued tokens at the REST API (RFC 7662), the system could mint its own JWTs after a user authenticates via the web frontend. Clients (web, CLI, and MCP facade) would present these JWTs in REST calls; the REST API would verify them locally without a round trip to an external provider.

docs.title: Current state of the system
docs.text: The web frontend authenticates users via Auth.js against GitHub or Google. Auth.js manages session state for the browser flow; no JWT is minted or consumed anywhere in the system today. For the CLI (a browserless client that calls the REST API directly), authentication is delegated to GitHub via the OAuth device authorization flow (RFC 8628); the CLI then presents the resulting GitHub token to the REST API, which introspects it. The MCP facade is a browserless client of the same shape and inherits the same pattern.

docs.title: Why not adopted
docs.text:
Introducing JWTs would require:

  • A token issuance path on the REST API, including signing key management and rotation.
  • A browserless acquisition flow, either user-driven copy/paste of a token minted in the web frontend, or a custom device-flow analogue against our own issuer.
  • Token revocation and lifecycle handling at the API layer, since one of introspection's benefits (immediate revocation by the identity provider) would no longer come for free.

The current team judged this disproportionate to the value gained, particularly because:

  • The CLI was built first under the same constraint; delegating browserless auth to GitHub's device flow solved the UX problem at zero implementation cost.
  • The REST API already supports introspection, so the MCP facade reuses existing infrastructure without modification.
  • Cross-client identity remains anchored at a single source (GitHub), removing the need for the system to maintain its own identity claims.

docs.title: Conditions to reconsider
docs.text:
This decision should be revisited if any of the following becomes true:

  • Introspection latency becomes a measurable bottleneck and caching proves insufficient.
  • The system requires identity claims or scopes that GitHub does not carry.
  • Dependency on GitHub's introspection endpoint availability becomes operationally unacceptable.
  • A second-class identity provider (beyond GitHub and Google) is introduced and federation becomes preferable to per-provider token validation.

docs.title: Implementation Costs if reconsidered
docs.text: Future contributors taking this on should expect to implement token issuance, signing key rotation, a browserless token acquisition UX (the painful part), local JWT verification at REST, and a revocation strategy. None of this is intractable; the current team simply judged the present arrangement adequate for the system's needs.

docs.title: 7. Threat Modeling
docs.text:
This section enumerates threats within the system's scope using the STRIDE framework (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege). The aim is to document the attack surface so new contributors can reason about changes, and to make existing mitigations and known gaps legible. Threats outside the scope of the system (credentialed insiders, social engineering, supply-chain compromise of dependencies) are noted only where they meaningfully shape design decisions.
